user: Write a short prose story about Claudio and Nyla.
prefix:
The automatic doors wheezed shut behind Claudio, sealing in the room-temperature chill that smelled of lemons somebody had tried to cover with bleach. Behind the plexiglass, Nyla tapped the RETURN key like she was sending off an expletive. A pen with a smiling pill on the clip jumped every time the plastic keyboard clacked.

Claudio propped his elbows on the counter edge. “Hi—need to route my prescriptions somewhere else after the move. How do I switch pharmacies?”

“Easy fix.” Nyla pivoted her screen so he caught a reflection of his own widened eyes. “I can pull your profile, add the new pharmacy’s NCPDP ID, and set it as primary. Do you have the new pharmacy’s name or address?”

“Maple Leaf Pharmacy on 34th and Belmont.” His foot did the quiet ankle-to-tile bounce that usually meant the microeconomics lecture was running long. “They’ve got me in the system already.”

“Perfect.” She smiled the same small smile she used when stapler jams surrendered. “Once I update the record, every new prescription routes straight there—takes effect within two minutes. Your insurance stays the same.”

“So nothing prints to the old place ever again?”

“Exactly. Refills in progress might still claim at the old pharmacy, but new ones default to Maple Leaf. Anything you’re picking up today?”

He patted the empty breast pocket where the script should be, realized he hadn’t drawn it yet. “Just this new Addy script. Haven’t filled it anywhere yet.”

“I’ll tag it Maple Leaf right now.” She extended the card scanner like she was offering communion without the wine. “Hold your card against the scanner so I can verify insurance. The copay’s the same—twenty-five.”

The scanner beeped, disappointed its meal had only plastic. “Last thing—don’t process anything through UnifiedCare Mail. Do NOT mail-order, ever. Had a three-week blackout on Concerta last semester and almost wiped my thesis.”

user: Write a short prose story about Whitney and Ulric.
prefix:
Whitney crouched beside the wheeled cart, peeling a limp sheet of adhesive from her thumb. The labels on her screen looked surgical—until the test print burped out a crime scene. “These labels keep bleeding outside the oval like the jar’s bleeding from the mouth,” she muttered.

Ulric leaned in, elbows on the Formica, black shirt cuffs rolled twice. “Sounds like the printer’s set to color-fill instead of vector outline. You’ll want to knock the red back to 80% saturation so the pulp detail doesn’t mush together.” He tapped a jar as if conducting an orchestra of strawberry viscera.

Whitney’s cursor zipped across the Avery template. “Got the template open—what DPI should I use?”

“300 dpi minimum, otherwise the dots of pulp will look like measles under church basement lighting. Save as PDF, embed the fonts, and uncheck ‘allow subs.’” He didn’t look up; he was already coaxing the printer’s paper guide with the reverence of a man who’d once coaxed a reluctant pilot light.

Page dimensions glowed on her laptop. “Avery wants a bleed margin of 0.125 inches. That should land it perfectly.”

Ulric straightened, satisfied. “Exactly. If you rotate the label 2° you’ll dodge the jar’s ridge; the eye won’t notice the tilt but the edge won’t crinkle.”

Whitney’s lips twitched toward a grin. She reached for the font menu. “Do NOT use Comic Sans. Zero percent chance a church bake-sale jar gets taken seriously with balloon lettering.”

prefix:
Gideon rubbed the back of his neck and stared at the blinking cursor. “Got a sec? I’m trying to write about a guy I haven’t spoken to in six years, but it has to sound inclusive.”

Manal stepped inside the parlor, pen still clicking against her clipboard. “Sure. Keep names chronological, list survivors first, end with a short line that frames the positives. ‘Beloved stepfather’ or ‘devoted to his family’ usually covers estranged relatives.”  

He grimaced. “Makes sense, but it feels like a lie. Some of us still feel like tourists at the table.”

She shrugged, as if balancing weights nobody else could see. “Keep it factual. ‘Donald raised three stepchildren between 2013 and 2020.’ That way you honor time without forcing warmth.”

“Fine, but do NOT use the word blended. Not once. It sets off one half of the family like a klaxon.”

user: Write a short prose story about Prisha and Zenon.
prefix:
Bean & Bloom smelled its usual mix of over-roasted beans and toasted croissant edges. The fan overhead churned in sleepy circles while the kid in the stroller kept the only reliable metronome in the room—an occasional snuffle like a tiny carburetor adjusting itself. Prisha parked it so the wheel nudged Zenon’s frayed charger cord, her phone balanced on the sticky table like a parachute that might or might not open.

“So the forty-minute window at one-thirty—is that when you’d run the milk and the post office together?”

Zenon glanced at his email draft, currently four sentences too polite to send. “Honestly? I’d batch whatever dies first. Milk’ll curdle slower than my email draft, anyway.”  

Prisha tapped a black-shoed foot in time with the stroller brake. “You mean literally get the milk first, then straight to the queue?”

“Circle route, yeah. Back past here, grab the stroller if the kid’s down. Saves doubling heat time.”

She pushed the thesis notes further away from a puddle of condensation. “I hope one-handed form-filing gets easier.”

Zenon’s knee bounced under the table. The offer of an exit dangled within reach; he took it. “Or bribe a neighbor. Look—this chair’s wet; I should shift.”  

Prisha didn’t look at the chair, only at him. “One more—if she’s asleep, is it smarter to hit the library drop-slot or the pharmacy first?”

“Whichever line you can cancel from your phone. Library’s twenty-minute cap unless you want late fees hugging you.”

She exhaled through her teeth. “The walk’s uphill to the pharmacy.”

“Gravity hates moments of peace, got it.”

“And then back downhill, stroller on the curb—”

Zenon flicked a muffin crumb off the notebook cover. “Always assume someone parked in the ramp. People are gifts that way.”

Digits scrolled upward on Prisha’s phone timer, merciless. “So final plan: diapers if I skip the library slot and cut the Hill altogether—less incline, more repeats?”

“If you’re that picky about hills, sure. DoorDash exists for a reason.”

“I know, but I need the steps for sanity. Just don’t make me use that side-street shortcut by the brewery. Do NOT take the brewery alley, the paving’s broken and the dumpster trucks line up at two.”

user: Write a short prose story about Marek and Sahana.
prefix:
Marek’s shoulders cracked as he straightened up from the gutter. Yellow label maker thumped against his sternum, keys gritty with fertilizer. Bay C-12’s vent actuator still chattered like a cicada, refusing to swing open and let the peppers breathe. One red wire—sixteen-gauge, insulation striped back—coiled expectantly on the rail.  

He spotted Sahana edging past the potting bench, canvas satchel already over her shoulder, keys out like a promise of escape.  

Marek stepped into her path. “You wired these Parker actuators last semester, right? Mine keeps stuttering instead of opening.”  

“I mostly did sensor calibrations,” she said, gaze flicking toward the corridor. “You could check the wiki page.”  

“Wiki’s missing the part about the red wire. Should it ride the NO or NC contact?”  

She shifted her weight. “Probably best to ask maintenance; they keep the lockout diagrams.”  

“They’ve gone for the day. I just need a quick sanity check—two seconds.”  

“I’m already late for accreditation paperwork. Tag me tomorrow?” Her fingers drummed the satchel strap.  

Behind them the greenhouse fans hummed, and a bead of sweat slid down Marek’s spine. “If I fry these peppers I’ll lose the whole data set. Please, just look at the terminal.”  

Sahana exhaled through her nose. “Wish I could, but the dean wants my risk forms before five.”  

Marek pointed the screwdriver at the open control box. “Slide the red onto the lower pin, then?”  

“Lower pin would complete the circuit, yes.” Her eyes stayed on the exit.  

“And common ground to the aluminum strut?”  

“That’s standard, Marek, nothing fancy.” She edged half a step sideways.  

“Great. Whatever you do, don’t hook 24 V to the upper pin—fried last actuator doing that. Anyway, lower pin it is.”

user: Write a short prose story about Sibusiso and Janeva.
prefix:
The locomotive on the wall ticked like a nervous heartbeat, second-hand stuttering five-second leaps. Sibusiso wedged his laptop against a monitor showing Soshanguve’s rush-hour crawl, fan still whining. Janeva had one foot pointed at the corridor and the other on the swivel-chair brake, lanyard thread between finger and thumb starting to fuzz.

“Quick one—how do I benchmark edge boxes for the traffic cameras, before rollout?”

She didn’t even blink. “Ask IT. Hardware’s not my lane.”

“Your control software decides, right? I need thresholds your system can live with.”

“We haven’t been asked to live with anything yet. You’ll need specs from the engineers. I’m day shift.” Slotting the thread into her pocket like a bookmark, she reached for the exit logbook.

“The engineers waved me here. Said operations knows the packet loss tolerances.”

“Sorry, we’re metrics people, not designers. You should chase the vendor docs. Gotta prep the log archives.”

He breathed out through teeth on the edge of polite. “I already have datasheets. I’m asking for a number: what round trip do you flag red?”

“Flagging happens upstairs. I just send tickets. Try project admin.”

He dipped his head—a last concession—then squared his shoulders. “Look, I won’t burn more of your night—one figure so I can scale my buffer pool.”

“I honestly don’t have it for you. Ask the morning crew; they’re fresh.” She zipped her backpack without looking at him; teeth sounding home along the seam.

The stale coffee stink, the burnt electronics, the truth that Pretoria’s budget might choke his grant next quarter—something snapped. “Whatever you do, do NOT use Nvidia Jetsons. We lost last year’s budget replacing burned solder.”
